title: India faces 100% tariff threat over Russian oil after US House vote
description: Trump’s tariff threat puts India’s Russian oil strategy- and its access to the US market - in a new bind.
body: A worker checks a sample of oil in Russia - India and China are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil For four years, India, one of the world's biggest oil importers, has turned Russia's war-driven disruption of global oil markets to its advantage. Russian crude, displaced from western markets after the invasion of Ukraine, has flowed instead to Indian refineries, often at attractive discounts. The arrangement has lowered the cost of one of India's biggest imports and given its refiners an abundant source of crude. Now that bargain is becoming a source of geopolitical risk. The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation giving President Donald Trump broad powers to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will now go to Trump to be signed into law. India and China are among those most exposed because both are major buyers of Russian oil. China accounted for half of Russia's crude exports, followed by India at 37%, Turkey at 5% and the EU at 5% between December 2022 and August 2026, according to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). Donald Trump and Narendra Modi at the White House in February 2025 Russia supplied 30.3% of India's crude imports in fiscal 2026, worth $40.8bn out of a total crude import bill of $134.7bn, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a Delhi-based think tank. In July, Russian crude accounted for more than half of India's imports. Other suppliers lagged far behind: the UAE accounted for 10.8% of India's July imports, Saudi Arabia 9.6%, Venezuela 6.3%, Brazil 5.5%, Oman 5.3% and the US 2.9%. Russia alone supplied more crude than all six combined. "The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices," says Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs GTRI. To be true, the economics of Russian oil have shifted. The crude no longer carries the steep discounts that made it particularly attractive to Indian refiners in the early years of the war, while competition for Russian barrels has intensified and shipping, insurance and sanctions risks have risen. "China and India, you better buy your oil and gas somewhere else," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal told reporters , externalafter the passage of the bill. These countries would normally have 180 days to cut Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington, but the president can shorten the deadline. India said in a statement that it was "monitoring further developments on this matter" and that it remained "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" for its people. "This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it added. India can find alternatives to Russian crude, but replacing it at scale would come at a price. S&P Global says alternative supplies, external can mean higher crude, freight and insurance costs, while longer shipping routes add to the burden. "The issue is not simply whether Russian barrels can be redirected to other buyers, but whether enough alternative crude is available to replace them without tightening the global market further," says Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at maritime intelligence firm Kpler. But the tariff would hit India elsewhere, too. The US is threatening tariffs on Indian exports to America, not a tax on Russian crude entering India. The impact would be felt through Indian exporters, the rupee, refinery margins and the trade balance. "This new bill could have major problematic impacts for India, and at the worst possible time, amid sensitive final-stage trade talks and shaky broader relations," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. "India has built some insulation to fend off the shocks of US tariffs through new trade deals with key markets in the EU and elsewhere, and through bolstering an already strong trade partnership with China. But [up to]100% tariffs from a critical export destination is real bad news, no matter how you slice it and even with successful hedging tactics." Indian refineries supplied some 70% of Russia's oil product imports in August The scale of that exposure is considerable. The US imported about $104bn of goods from India in 2025, while two-way US-India trade in goods and services was roughly $240bn, according to the US Trade Representative. India's exports to the US include electronics, pharmaceuticals, machinery, jewellery, chemicals, textiles and petroleum products. In 2025, electrical and electronic equipment alone accounted for about $25.8bn of Indian exports to America, pharmaceuticals about $9.7bn and machinery about $7.2bn. The new threat comes after an earlier round of Trump tariffs on Indian goods, which peaked at 50% in 2025 before being reduced. That creates an uncomfortable calculation for Delhi: how much should India pay for Russian crude before the savings are outweighed by the risk to its exports to the US? There is no simple answer. It will depend on the Russian discount, global crude prices, freight and insurance costs, the tariff Trump ultimately imposes, and whether Washington offers exemptions or reaches a broader settlement with Delhi. The picture gets more complicated once the crude is refined. India is not merely a buyer: its refineries turn Russian crude into fuels that can then be exported. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have forced the world's once-largest oil-products exporter to import fuel. In August, imports hit a record 172,000 tonnes, more than seven times the p

title: 'My mother apologised': A survivor's journey after genital mutilation
description: Sara Kahsai was 29 when she found out she had FGM as a baby.
body: Sara Kahsai wants all survivors of FGM to seek help and not suffer alone Sara Kahsai grew up in Sudan but moved to Birmingham, England, in 2022 after a marrying a bus driver from the city. But as she settled into married life and her new home, she was coming to terms with a life-changing discovery. Sara realised she was a victim-survivor of Female Genital Mutiliation (FGM), a procedure she had endured as a young girl. She was floored by the revelation and, not least, the excruciating pain she was now beginning to fully understand. "The shock was massive," she said. "It made it difficult with my physical relationship with my husband - but he was very kind and very patient with me." Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation Sara turned to the one person she knew must have orchestrated it - her mother - and asked her why. "I was a baby. It was the culture to do it for everybody," she said her mother, still living in Africa, told her. "When I spoke to my mum she was really upset and she apologised to me." FGM involves the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons, and is practiced in some parts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia. It also happens within some migrant communities in the UK, where it is illegal and treated as child abuse. It is also against the law to take a girl abroad for FGM. Reasons include social acceptance, religion, misconceptions about hygiene and preserving a girl or woman's virginity. The Home Office website cites World Health Organisation figures showing three million girls undergo some form, external of the procedure every year in Africa alone. The mum received help for her FGM after she found out she was pregnant When Sara fell pregnant, she finally told health professionals she had endured FGM as a child. She was immediately referred to the specialist FGM Clinic, run by midwives at Birmingham Women's Hospital. Midwife Renata Hanif deals with around 200 cases each year and says her job is to ensure the wellbeing of women and safeguard unborn children. "Some types of female circumcision can affect the vaginal delivery," she said. They offer deinfibulation - a procedure that can be carried out during pregnancy that to separate fused tissue and enable safer births. What is FGM, where does it happen and why? Victim-survivors of FGM can also experience difficulty with urinating and menstruating, the midwife said. Women are more prone to infections and sepsis, and can suffer from severe and ongoing pain, as well having to deal with psychological trauma, anxiety and depression. Many patients find it hard to talk to her about what's happened to them, Hanif said. "It is very difficult, very emotional. It's very difficult for the woman to actually come forward and to come to the clinic, attend the clinic, and have a conversation with me as well," she said. "I explain to them that I'm here to help and I try to explain to them what happened to them when they were a child." She said most women leave the clinic with a better understanding of how they have been affected and how they can take back control of their bodies. "We talk about every part, what that part is there for and what's been removed and what cause for concern and what effect this will have for the rest of her life," Hanif said. Counselling is also offered as well as information on how partners and husbands can support them. Midwife Renata Hanif runs the FGM centre at Birmingham Women's Hospital In 2015, children's charity Barnardo's set up the National FGM Centre to help better protect women and girls. It works to prevent FGM, raise awareness of it and support those affected. The centre said schools are legally required to teach pupils about FGM and the law surrounding it as part of relationships and sex education. But how it is delivered can vary between schools. It's also not mandatory for it to be taught in primary schools and they want to see that change. "For us, a huge part of tackling FGM is prevention," Roma Ullah, from the centre, said. "Yes, a conviction, a prosecution, can provide justice, accountability and send strong messages into communities, but by then the harm has already happened." Sara says that if she knew help was out there, she would have sought help sooner In April, the government held its first dedicated FGM Summit in a decade, to discuss ways to better protect women and girls. Among improvements on the way are new guidelines to help identify girls at risk of being taken abroad for FGM. Sara wants to urge other women in a similar position to take immediate action. "I have a message to all ladies who've had FGM," she said. "When they come to the UK it is different. There's help here - go to their GP, seek help, ask for help. "If I knew I could seek help I would not have waited until I was expecting... because I did suffer a lot before." If you have been affected by the contents of the article, support is available through the BBC Action Line website. title: Review of legal framework launched in wake of Eleanor Donaldson trial
description: The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and end by the end of February 2027.
body: Lady Eleanor Donaldson arriving at Newry Crown Court for a hearing in 2025 Stormont's justice and health ministers have launched a joint review of the legal framework on trials of the facts in the wake of the Donaldson trial, BBC News NI understands. That's according to a letter from the Department of Justice's assembly liaison officer. Eleanor Donaldson, wife of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds. The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and conclude by the end of February 2027. The letter to Stormont's justice committee said the move came in the wake of "public concern and interest" on trials of the facts, and that work would now take place on the terms of reference of the review. Both the Department of Justice and the Department of Health have been contacted for comment. A trial of the facts is an option that is open to prosecutors if a court determines that a person is unfit to stand trial and criminal proceedings cannot go ahead. It takes the place of a criminal trial and is used to determine whether an accused committed the acts alleged. It cannot result in a conviction, but if the court is not satisfied that the accused committed the acts alleged, then he/she will be acquitted. The procedure is allowed for in legislation by Article 49A of the Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986. The mechanism is not used often but one high-profile example was in the trial of former IRA leader Ivor Bell in 2019. In some ways, it is similar to a normal criminal trial - the prosecution puts its evidence against the defendant before a judge and jury in a courtroom. However, perhaps the key difference, is that the accused does not play a part in proceedings, and does not even need to be in court. That was the case with Eleanor Donaldson, who was not present on any day of the four-week trial in which evidence was heard against her and her husband. However, in a trial of the facts the accused will be represented by a legal team and their lawyers can question the witnesses, challenge the evidence and make legal submissions on their behalf. Ian Turkington KC represented Eleanor Donaldson during her trial of the facts, cross-examining witnesses and issuing closing remarks on behalf of his client towards the end of the trial. Then there is the major differences in what the outcome can be in a trial of the facts. Instead of being asked to return a verdict of guilty or not guilty, the jury are asked to decide whether or not the accused committed the offence with which they were charged. The focus is on what they are alleged to have physically done - not their state of mind at the time. In a normal criminal trial, a jury would be invited to decide whether or not a defendant had the mental faculties required to be guilty of the offence as well. The standard of proof remains the same - a jury must be sure beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused committed the acts alleged. The accused cannot be convicted but they can be acquitted if the jury decide they didn't commit the acts alleged. title: Inside the 'scariest house on Rightmove'
description: The station house in Bleasby, dating back to the 1840s, has been dubbed the "scariest" on Rightmove.
body: It is believed the "creepy doll" left standing in the corner of a bedroom had captured people's imaginations An old station house that is up for auction in Nottinghamshire has had unexpected attention after being dubbed the "scariest house on Rightmove". The property in Bleasby dates back to the 1840s, when the railway station opened, and would have been home to the station masters who were responsible for opening and closing the station barriers. Although steeped in local history, the eerie character of the house in its listing images is what seems to have gathered interest. Area manager at Auction House Notts & Derby, Jonathan Way, said he believed it was a "creepy doll" left standing in the corner of a bedroom that had captured people's imaginations. The house had been empty for some time and a number of break-ins eventually led to the downstairs windows being boarded up, which had not helped the atmosphere, Way said. He added the house had been left untouched before the images were taken for the listing. Speaking about his first visit, alongside his colleagues, Way said: "It was a little bit unsettling. "It was all boarded up downstairs, there wasn't any natural light downstairs. The lights weren't working either so we had to use phone lights to move around. "Upstairs wasn't too bad but the doll and the pram were a little bit creepy. "I definitely wasn't expecting that when I walked up the stairs." Part of the old station house in Bleasby can be seen in this old image The property caught the attention of the content creator behind the Housing Horrors TikTok account, where a video was posted dubbing the old station house the "scariest house on Rightmove". The social media account regularly shares videos of property listings, often highlighting some of the strangest looking houses on the market across the country. But the post had not put people off, Way said. The area manager said the property had still proven to be very popular. He said: "You get the odd quirky [property] but I've not really done one like that before. "It's a really old station house. "It's still got the original brickwork and the design in side obviously hasn't been touched for a number of years." The property is due to go under the hammer on 28 September. title: A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel
description: Can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
body: A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport. Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament. At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren". Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share. Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team. "That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz. "Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids." It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though. After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television. In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina. To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history. "That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky. "That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future." But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel. The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised? Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023 Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023. Their run was no fluke. The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level. They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros. Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers. But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart. Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer. After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise. Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg. Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated. Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States. All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim. "It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup. "We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers. "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team." Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet. "The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history. "They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way." Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other. When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do. They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football. While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally. The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team. Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity an

title: 'I was given electric shocks to knock the homosexuality out of my brain'
description: People who were subjected to electric shocks to change their sexuality demand the government apologises.
body: Norman Goodman underwent controversial electric shock therapy More victims of controversial electric shock therapy used to try to change their sexuality have come forward to call on the government to investigate the historical "scandal". They spoke out after the BBC revealed that more than 260 people had been subjected to the discredited treatment at NHS hospitals in the 1960s and 1970s. The people, who are now in their 70s and 80s, said they had been left physically and emotionally traumatised by their experiences. And while the government said it would be drafting legislation to ban "aversion therapy", ten months on, the people spoken to by the BBC said they were still yet to receive an apology for what they had endured. The BBC's investigation uncovered evidence that LGBT+ patients were subjected to electric shock aversion therapy in NHS hospitals across England. Patients were shown images associated with same-sex attraction while being given painful electric shocks in an attempt to change their sexuality. Norman came forward following an earlier BBC investigation into electric shock therapy Norman Goodman, 75, said that from childhood he felt more like a girl than a boy, and told his parents that he wanted to be female. He was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in Manchester when he was 18, in the late 1960s. He told the BBC doctors said they would try to make it easier for him, but he was given electric shocks. "I didn't realise it was to knock the homosexuality out of my brain," he told the BBC. He said he was strapped to a bed and electrodes were put on his arms, legs and on either side of his head, before electricity was passed through them. " It was absolutely terrible. They started shocking me. I was really frightened. "And next thing I knew, it was as though I didn't know where I was. "I didn't even know who I was. I was very weak. I had no appetite and no energy. " Norman said he remembered NHS staff trying to make him change his mannerisms, telling him to walk and behave in a more masculine way. But the treatment did not change who he was. Debbie Burley told the BBC her grandfather, Arthur James Emberton, also went through electric shock therapy. She only found out about 20 years ago what he had been through, long after he had died. He had been a respected businessman from Cheshire, running his own cheese company. In 1965, aged 61, he appeared at Nantwich magistrates' court after being charged with indecent assault. He had been caught kissing a boy in a doorway. The court heard he was given probation on the condition that he sought medical treatment. Court documents show that treatment had already begun before he was sentenced. According to Debbie, Arthur's wife divorced him, he was forced out of the family business - which was later sold - and spent much of the rest of his life living alone in YMCA accommodation. While the documents do not indicate what treatment he received, family members later learned he had gone through electric shock aversion therapy. Debbie said the consequences were catastrophic. "He never rebuilt his life," she said. "He carried that shame for the rest of his life. "As an adult, I now understand the enormous injustice done to him," she said. "He was wronged by the state, the medical system and the attitudes of the time." Another man said his experience had "broken him" Another man who contacted the BBC said he was 16 when he realised he was attracted to men. "I thought I was the only one in the world," said the man, who asked to remain anonymous because, even though he is in his late 80s, he has never told his family that he is gay. He said his parents took him to a doctor, who prescribed testosterone tablets. But, he said, the medication made him aggressive and unwell. So he was referred for electric shock treatment at a mental health unit. The treatment took place once a week for about two years. "The shock treatment itself was terrible," he said. "And after the shocks, I was like a zombie. "I'd be going to sleep at all times of the day at home and I'd wake up crying." Doctors told him the treatment would "straighten him out". But, he said, it did not change the way he felt. He said the treatment had "broken him". "I'm still broken now," he said. Hel Spandler, Professor of mental Health studies at the University of Lancashire Most of the people who had electric shock aversion therapy were men. But records show some women and, in some cases, children were also subjected to the treatment. People were referred by their families, schools, churches, or the courts. Hel Spandler, Prof of Mental health studies at the University of Lancashire, said the figure of 260 was likely to be far lower than the true number. "Sadly, I think this figure is quite conservative and it's likely that considerably more LGBT people were affected," they said. "We need to remember that, at the time, being gay or trans was considered a mental disorder, and this type of aversion therapy was one of many so-called therapies used to try and 'treat' it. "While it was probably the most controversial method, for over a decade it was an accepted practice in the NHS. "Indeed NHS hospitals in every major city in England had aversion therapy suites precisely for this purpose." This video can not be played Shock Treatment: The Gay Therapy Scandal Professor Spandler said there was evidence the practice was also exported to other countries, and that hundreds more people may have undergone the treatment. Many of those affected are now elderly, and some have spent decades carrying the trauma in silence. They are calling not only for a full investigation into historic conversion practices, but also for accountability and a comprehensive ban on all forms of conversion therapy. But a bill currently working its way through Parliament, the draft Conversion Practices Bill, has met with opposition from some religious groups. The Bishop of Le

title: St Leger win has removed Osborne's fear of failure
description: St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her now she has won a British Classic, becoming the first woman to do so.
body: Osborne had her first season as an apprentice in 2020 and rode her first Classic four years later St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her after she became the first woman to win a British Classic. The 24-year-old said that despite wanting to achieve "so much more", her victory at Doncaster on Saturday means she will always be able to look back and think her career was "worth it". Osborne said the sport can be "very lonely" - she estimates she drives 65,000 miles a year, often alone - and she has suffered some serious falls, breaking numerous bones. But she told BBC Sport that winning one of British Flat racing's five Classics had been a dream since she was five. She has now fulfilled it. While racing is a sport where men and women compete against one another, opportunities have not been equal. Only six female jockeys have had rides in British Classics in 250 years, totalling 12 rides, according to the National Horseracing Museum. They are Gay Kelleway (The Oaks, 1986; The Oaks, 1987), Alex Greaves (The Derby, 1996; 1,000 Guineas, 1996), Hayley Turner (The Derby, 2012) Josephine Gordon (1,000 Guineas, 2017), Hollie Doyle (The Oaks, 2021; St Leger, 2021; The Oaks, 2022) and Saffie Osborne (2,000 Guineas, 2024; 1,000 Guineas, 2026; St Leger, 2026). "It has been a male-dominated sport for an extremely long time, and I suppose it's becoming less and less of a conversation, which is quite nice," she said. "When people talk about the firsts of what women have done, I think to have my own one is quite special. "I think it's also quite poignant because there's so few left of first things for women to do in this sport." This video can not be played 'I did it because I loved it' - St Leger winner Osborne On Saturday's groundbreaking win, she added: "That sort of fear of failure has sort of disappeared. However much more I want to achieve, and I want to achieve so much more, it's kind of like I can always look back on my career and know that it was all worth it. "I got to achieve what I always dreamed of achieving." Osborne's ride on Highwayman in the St Leger was her first for trainer Joseph O'Brien, and only came about because of an injury to regular jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle. She acknowledged that the success of a jockey is dependent on "being chosen", but is adamant that her gender isn't a factor in the opportunities she gets. "I don't feel like in my position now that I'm ever looked at any differently because I'm a woman," she said. "Any jockey, when you're starting out, it takes years to gain respect and be looked at as a person that people would want to use. And I don't think my gender at this point would have had anything to do with it. "Hopefully Saturday will open more doors. But when it comes to me as a female jockey, I don't think I'm viewed any differently within the industry." Osborne also said she is treated as "one of the lads" in the weighing room, and has never experienced sexism and misogyny unlike other female jockeys, including Bryony Frost. Jockey Robbie Dunne was banned from racing for 18 months, with three months suspended, for bullying fellow rider Frost in 2021, which was later cut to 10 months on appeal. Having ridden 60 winners since the start of May, Osborne is currently sitting eighth in the Flat Jockeys Championship, and is open about dreaming of being champion jockey in the future. She would be the first female jockey to achieve that. "You wouldn't be a jockey if you didn't want to be champion jockey one day. I think this is the first year that maybe I truly believe that I could one day," she said. "It's been a phenomenal year that's been topped off by Saturday. But I'm very lucky. I have a very good agent [Tony Hind] and agents are so important in this sport. He's got an amazing book of jockeys, the likes of Ryan Moore, William Buick, Billy Loughnane. And I'm very lucky to be on his team. "He makes champion jockeys, he's had a lot of them. And yeah, I would love to be the next one on the list." title: 'No doubt' that climate change played role in Nepal-Tibet flood, study finds
description: More than 1,400 people were killed and thousands are missing following the deluge on 26 August.
body: Thousands of people are dead or missing after massive floods and landslides tore through the Nepal-Tibet border last month A study has found that climate change had contributed to the glacier collapse that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border. More than 1,400 people were killed and thousands are missing following the deluge on 26 August. There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Friederike Otto, a climatologist at Imperial College London and one of the study's authors. The World Weather Attribution study, published on Thursday, said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses. Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing. Scientists had previously said that the floods were caused by the collapse of a glacier slope near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas. The large chunk of glacier hit the bottom of a valley with such force that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to United States Geological Survey (USGS) data. The World Weather Attribution study said climate change was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", but it was not the only cause of the disaster. According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (34.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate". Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability. Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year. This combination of activities "may have interacted to amplify the compound event," the study said. This video can not be played Watch: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods? A magnitude 7.8 earthquake that struck the area in 2015 and triggered a rock-ice avalanche, could have also weakened the underlying rock mass, according to the study. However, authorities said they could not confirm that earthquake's exact impact on the glacier collapse last month. Another co-author of the report, Utrecht University mountain hydrologist Walter Immerzeel, told reporters that the area was a "geologically vulnerable slope". Immerzeel said it was "potentially weakened by the 2015 earthquake" and "destabilised further" by glacier and permafrost retreat. In the wake of the disaster, Nepali authorities have called for global efforts to tackle climate change, saying the country is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse emissions yet one of the most vulnerable places to the effects of global warming. In his first foreign trip as Nepali Prime Minister, Balendra Shah is set to appear at United Nations General Assembly in New York next week to talk about the recent disaster and climate justice. title: Boy abducted by mum has renewed 'sense of purpose'
description: Alex Batty, who vanished aged 11 in 2017, says a new job has given him renewed purpose.
body: Alex Batty has been working at a waste management site for three months Alex Batty, who disappeared for six years after being abducted by his mother as a child, has described feeling a renewed "sense of purpose" after finding work. Batty, from Oldham, was declared missing by his grandmother in 2017, aged 11, after his mother and grandfather failed to return him from a holiday in Spain and instead moved to France He spent the following years in isolation before he was spotted by a delivery driver in December 2023 in the foothills of the Pyrenees in the south-west of the country. Batty, who is now 20, said his job at a waste management company had given his young family financial security. It has been a whirlwind couple of years for Batty, whose teenage years were spent living as a nomad in France. His mother, Melanie, who was not his legal guardian and was heavily influenced by conspiracy theories, told him to throw away his passport. They lived off-grid and he did not attend school. Alex Batty was just 11 years old when he went missing When he was discovered, he was heading for Toulouse with just a skateboard and €100 in cash. Alex returned to live with his grandmother Susan Caruana, his legal guardian, in Oldham shortly afterwards, but found himself out of work for a long time. "I've been used to having a job because I started working when I was young," he told the BBC. "So, when I couldn't find one it did not feel right." When Batty appeared on BBC Breakfast to discuss his abduction, he revealed he was one of 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training. Daniel Carolan, a manager at SUEZ UK, happened to be listening to the interview and ended up reaching out. Daniel Carolan contacted Alex Batty after seeing him on BBC Breakfast Carolan said: "We were talking in the office about how we can make our recruitment better and how we can find these people. "After two minutes of listening to Alex speak I knew he was desperate to find work and I felt he deserved an opportunity." Three months on, Batty said it was "a great feeling" knowing he was in employment. "It was a lot of pressure when I didn't have a job because I have a family. "You're sitting there doing everything you can but [applications] are all online and you can't show anyone what you can do." He added: "I've got a baby and my missus, and without a job there is a pressure to support them financially. "So it gives us security, and I know I can provide for my family." title: Low-cost food pantry awarded £272k lottery grant
description: Oasis Hub Bath said the funding will cover its main operating costs over the next three years.
body: Alongside the pantries, Oasis Hub Bath in the city centre hosts multiple community projects and services A community hub and food pantry has been awarded £272,702, which managers say will cover its main costs for the next three years. Oasis Hub Bath, which opened in the city centre in 2018, has two affordable food pantries that support around 600 people each week. Community director Jo Dolby said the funds awarded by the National Lottery Community Fund "will cover the majority of our core operating costs over the next three years". "It will also enable us to develop additional services that respond to emerging needs in our local community," she said. "The pantry basically keeps us going", said a pantry member who did not want to be named. "No matter what's going on financially, whatever stresses and strains we've got, it's always an accessible price point for us to be able to come and be sorted for the week." Family 'devastated' as missing girl case stays closed Elderly woman dies in bus collision on high street Wonky bridge to remain closed for months The hub also offers support sessions with organisations such as Citizens Advice, as well as health checks with partner healthcare organisations. Another member of the food pantry said that it helped them with their electricity bills. "I saw someone here who helped me, it was amazing. She was so helpful, non-judgemental," they said. Oasis Hub Bath opened in the city centre in 2018 To be eligible to join the Pantry, members must have an annual household income of less than £18,000 or be struggling to afford food, and live in eligible areas of Bath. There are two membership tiers, £5 per week for 6 items or £7.50 per week for 10 items, which includes access to chilled and cupboard food, toiletries, and household items. Some items with shorter shelf lives, including fruit and vegetables, are available for free. Sam, another member, said that coming to the pantry had "changed my life for the good and saved my life". "I came to the pantry one day and there was a nurse here. She checked my blood pressure and said it was absolutely rocketing. I went straight to hospital, put on an ECG machine and they found out that I had very high blood pressure," he said. "Coming here saved my life, so I am so grateful to the pantry and all their staff because I wouldn't be here today without that". title: Energy firm unveils new slimline pylons designed 'with Welsh landscape in mind' after backlash
description: Green Gen Cymru says the 22m high single-pole structure was considerably shorter than traditional steel pylons.
body: A computer simulated image of what Green Gen Cymru's new pylon could look like An energy firm facing backlash over plans for new power lines has unveiled what it has described as a "slim and compact" pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind". Green Gen Cymru said the 22m (72ft) high single-pole structure was considerably shorter than traditional steel pylons, with the aim of "limiting visual impact". The firm's design has been commissioned for use on two of its three planned routes for upgrading the electricity grid across mid and west Wales. The Campaign for the Protection of Rural Wales said it was "still a major piece of infrastructure in the countryside". A Green Gen Cymru graphic showing their proposed pylon routes Green Gen's proposals have previously sparked protests and legal action, as well as a pledge from the Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government to prohibit the use of large-scale steel pylons. The company said its new pylon had been inspired by "monopole designs commonly used across Europe". "Monopoles are single-pole structures designed to carry significant electricity network capacity within a slim and compact profile," it explained. The company had previously proposed using 27m tall steel pylons, whereas this new design would be nearer 22m. Wooden-pole alternatives are around 12m high but can carry less electricity. Using monopoles rather than wooden ones would mean fewer overhead lines are needed, the company said, reducing impacts on farmland and scenery. They have argued that relying solely on putting cables underground is prohibitively expensive and disruptive. The new monopoles will be used on the firm's Towy Usk, external and Towy Teifi, external projects - as part of a "toolkit" which also includes wood poles, underground cables and traditional pylons. A prototype is expected to be ready to be installed in early 2027 for communities to see. Georgia Rollison can already see a pylon from her bedroom window The firm has issued computer-simulated images of what its new pylons could look like. BBC News asked passers-by in Carmarthen what they made of the design. Georgia Rollinson, 27, said she had a pylon outside her bedroom window and thought these looked "a little bit better". "I think I'd prefer that to one of the others. It might blend in better," she said. "If people want to live in the modern world with the television and internet then they have to have some sacrifices somewhere - even if it is a pylon in the middle of a field." Anthony Read, 69, said: "They certainly do look smaller and better but ideally put them underground if you can." He claimed: "It's all down to cost but if something's hidden it's better for the environment." Four of the structures would be required per kilometre Phillip Richardson, 78, asked: "Why spend money replacing [pylons] with something that's only marginally better? "I can't see them being better for the environment - it's a waste of money and could be better spent." Robin Daniels, 58, said they looked "a lot better than the traditional ones you see across the landscape". "We've got to decarbonise and the electricity's got to move somehow," he added. "Burying the cables is expensive so if this is an alternative to make it a bit less of an eyesore, it's probably a good idea." Phillip Richardson felt it was a waste of time and money to come up with a new pylon design Green Gen hopes to build three major powerline routes connecting onshore windfarms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network. It says it will invest nearly £1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire. But it has faced considerable backlash in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners recently taking the company to court. Plaid Cymru also campaigned against pylons ahead of winning May's Senedd election, promising in its manifesto to have "a clear presumption in favour of undergrounding" new power lines. "Overhead alternatives" would only be allowed "where installation is via low wooden poles or equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure". Green Gen Cymru's plans have faced considerable backlash in some communities Dr Jonathan Dean, from the Campaign for the Protection of Rural Wales, said the new design would not be enough to placate opponents of the firm's plans. "It is still a major piece of infrastructure in the countryside," he argued, while separate proposals for new transmission lines under consideration by the National Energy System Operator (NESO) could render Green Gen's plans "utterly redundant". Farmer Dyfan Walters, who lives near one of the company's proposed pylon paths on the outskirts of Llandovery in Carmarthenshire, said "undergrounding is the only option that we would consider and that is very much aligned to the Plaid Cymru policy". While the new pylons would still be unacceptable to many, he said the fact the company had been forced to change its original plans should be viewed as "a win for the community". Guto Davies of Green Gen Cymru said the announcement was an exciting moment for the company Guto Davies, head of external affairs at Green Gen Cymru, said a range of factors had led the firm to look for an alternative pylon design including "engineering and environmental implications, the community feedback and of course the political landscape in which we're operating". "We've tried to test ourselves to find an innovative approach" that would help "deliver for Wales' economic, productivity and decarbonisation ambitions whilst also making sure we build around the needs of the communities that are hosting this infrastructure". Stephen Rowlands, the company's head of construction and supply chain said there was "a real opportunity for Welsh industry to play a leading role" in developing and delivering the new pylons. title: Rare tree offspring given lifeline at Scottish botanic garden
description: Logan Botanic Garden is helping save a species native to Robinson Crusoe Island in the South Pacific.
body: Logan Botanic Garden has been described as "Scotland's most exotic garden" The offspring of one of the world's rarest trees has been given a new home in south-west Scotland as conservationists step up efforts to save the species from extinction. Two seedlings from the last known wild dendroseris neriifolia tree have arrived at Logan Botanic Garden in Dumfries and Galloway after an international rescue effort involving experts in Chile and the UK. The species, native to Robinson Crusoe Island in the South Pacific, has been pushed to the brink by habitat loss, invasive species and repeated wildfires. Conservationists hope the move will provide a vital safeguard for the future of a plant that now survives in the wild as a single tree clinging to a cliff face. Garden's sapphire tower flower begins to bloom Giant plants make epic journey to new home The dendroseris neriifolia, a rare tree daisy found only on Chile's Robinson Crusoe Island, has suffered a dramatic decline over recent decades. By 1980, only eight wild specimens remained, and although reintroduction projects were launched in the early 2000s, the breakdown of protection measures in 2017 left the species vulnerable once again to invasive plants and grazing animals. Today, the last surviving wild tree is supported by ropes on a steep volcanic outcrop to prevent it from falling. In May this year, 29 seeds were collected from the lone tree and sent to the Millennium Seed Bank at Kew Wakehurst. The species is native to Robinson Crusoe Island in the South Pacific Eight seedlings successfully germinated, with two now transferred to Logan Botanic Garden, where the climate is considered particularly suitable for rare Chilean plants. The remaining seedlings will stay at Kew. Richard Baines, curator at Logan, described the arrival as a significant moment and said the garden could play an important role in learning more about the species and helping secure its future. "Experience shows that plant species from the Juan Fernández Islands do well at Logan," he said. "This is the start of an exciting new period. "Creating a safe place for these seedlings, getting to know them, and learning more about their adaption to different environments, gives us the chance to contribute so much more." What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? Scientists involved in the project said the international collaboration offered a rare opportunity to prevent the extinction of a unique plant lineage and preserve part of the natural heritage of the Juan Fernández archipelago. Diego Penneckamp, a scientist at Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, said saving the species was a "race against time". "This international collaboration to support the last remaining individual could prevent the extinction of a species that represents a unique lineage with its own natural history," he said. title: International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
description: The government wants to reduce net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.
body: Australia will cut immigration by cracking down on international students and backpackers, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration. Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification. Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK. The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control". For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over." There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said. PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said. In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028. On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider". Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters. He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year. Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year. Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year. For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia. New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m. That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100. Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services. One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years. The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy". In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas. Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas. It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK. Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country". "The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent". title: Balaclava boys on electric bikes: How to tackle the problem?
description: The sight of masked young men on electric bikes or motorcycles is becoming increasingly familiar - what can be done about it?
body: A member of the public posted this image of young men in the Pentland Hills after witnessing a horse being spooked From the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh to the streets of the country's biggest cities, a common menace is causing irritation, alarm and in some cases even death. The sight of young men, their identities hidden by black balaclavas, tearing around on electric bikes or scooters is becoming a familiar one. The picture above was taken by a man who posted on social media about "morons on electric bikes" scaring a nearby horse, external as they rode illegally on public footpaths. Aside from being showered with gravel churned up by the "gobby" miscreants, no one came to harm that day, but others have not been so lucky. This video can not be played Warning: Contains distressing scenes. Dashcam footage shows the aftermath of the crash that killed a pedestrian in Sunderland Earlier this year, a court was shown distressing dashcam footage of the moment a masked 18-year-old on an electric motorbike ploughed into a woman on a pedestrian crossing in Sunderland. Gloria Stephenson, 86, died at the scene. The rider - Billy Stokoe, who had taken cannabis and was using his mobile at the time of the crash - was jailed for more than six years for causing death by dangerous driving. Few would dispute that illegal e-bikes and scooters are a growing problem, but what can be done about it? Here are some of the options. The term e-bike is often used loosely to cover a range of different vehicles. Strictly speaking it refers to an electrically assisted pedal cycle (an EAPC) where an electric motor kicks in to take the strain off the rider while pedalling. By law, the motor cuts out at 15.5mph (25km/h) and its continuous power is capped at 250 watts. But these safeguards are easily bypassed by "tuning kits" or software hacks that make them capable of running much faster, sometimes in excess of 40mph. A quick search of online marketplaces reveals all sorts of modifications on offer, often shipped from eastern Europe, including motorbike-style twist grip throttles which allow the rider to accelerate without pedalling. Modifications for e-bikes are openly advertised on online marketplaces Then there are electric dirt bikes from manufacturers such as Sur-Ron which look like mountain bikes but are capable of about 50mph - and 70mph or more if modified. Unlike legal e-bikes they require a licence and insurance to be used in public spaces or on roads. E-scooters are also popular - despite it currently being illegal to ride them on public roads or pavements except in certain rental zones. What they all have in common is that they are expensive, ranging from a few hundred to several thousands of pounds, and modifications can cost hundreds of pounds more on top. Seizing and destroying them represents a significant penalty. A new law and rules introduced this summer gave police in England and Wales greater powers to seize illegal vehicles, and without the need for a formal warning if they are being used in an anti-social manner. They can also now be crushed within 48 hours. In Scotland, ministers say they are in favour of increasing police seizure powers, although they point out bikes can already be seized under certain circumstances. Catching the offenders is a problem for the police - it's a crime where its very nature means the suspects have a fast and highly manoeuvrable method of escape. A patrol car can easily be evaded by heading down a narrow alleyway or through bollards. David Kennedy from the Scottish Police Federation says more dangerous tactics are also employed. "These individuals on these bikes will come up one-way streets the wrong way so there's no way a police officer in a car or even on a motorbike would be safe to follow them," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast. The Metropolitan Police say their fleet of electric dirt bikes is helping to cut crime Some forces across the UK have responded to the challenge by setting up specialised units backed up by drones In parts of inner city London, Metropolitan Police officers have been equipped with a fleet of 25 Sur-Ron dirt bikes - partly funded with proceeds of crime money. As part of a crackdown targeting mobile phone thefts - which in London often involve such bikes - they claim it has helped cut offences by 13,000 in a year. This video can not be played Gwent Police, in south Wales, have made use of drones to target illegal e-bikes A number of forces have successfully used drones to track illegal e-bike riders rather than engaging in risky pursuits. Officers monitor suspects from above, then their colleagues are directed to move in on foot to make seizures and arrests. In Devon and Cornwall officers have also sprayed illegal riders and their bikes with SmartWater - a forensic marking product that contains a unique chemical code which becomes visible using ultraviolet light. One of the most sinister aspects of e-bike misuse is that riders often wear black balaclavas or "ballys". Whether it is a practical attempt to hide their identity or part of a youth sub-culture, there is no doubt that many people find the sight of masked youths intimidating. The debate about the appropriateness of wearing balaclavas in public places goes wider than e-bikes, encompassing anti-social behaviour, crime and some anti-immigration protests. A group of boys pictured on top of a former Debenhams store in Nottingham is an example of behaviour that has prompted the restrictions on face coverings New restrictions introduced just this week under Operation Reclaim in Nottingham give police and council officers the power to order people to remove face coverings, backed up by £70 fixed penalty notices. Exemptions apply for religious, medical and certain other legitimate reasons. title: Afghan inquiry into alleged SAS war crimes has already cost £58m, MoD figures show
description: The inquiry has been running for more than three and a half years but has yet to publish any findings.
body: The SAS carried out night raids with Afghan special forces to target the Taliban An inquiry into allegations British Special Forces murdered unarmed Afghan civilians has cost UK taxpayers £58m, figures from the Ministry of Defence (MoD) show. When the inquiry was launched in 2023, its chair Lord Justice Haddon-Cave said it would aim to report, "at least on an interim basis", within 12-18 months. However, the inquiry has now been running for more than three and a half years, and has yet to publish any findings. In a statement, the inquiry said its work was "greater and more complex than it originally envisaged". It added that delays by the MoD in disclosing information had also affected the timetable. The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan (IIRTA) was established to investigate alleged war crimes committed by soldiers serving with the Special Air Service between 2010 and 2013, during so called night raids targeting the Taliban. These include allegations the SAS murdered detainees and unarmed civilians, including children, during operations. It was set up by the former defence secretary, Ben Wallace, in the wake of allegations first reported by BBC Panorama, in 2022. SAS unit repeatedly killed Afghan detainees, BBC finds SAS had golden pass to get away with murder, inquiry told SAS war crime evidence suppressed, inquiry hears While much of the inquiry's work has been carried out in closed sessions to protect the identities of serving personnel, it has published some evidence on its website. It has already heard evidence from senior UK military personnel who have said they believed the SAS carried out extra judicial killings of Afghan civilians. It has also heard concerns about the secrecy in which the SAS operated and that previous investigations into the allegations were ended prematurely. The inquiry is investigating alleged war crimes by SAS soldiers in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013 The inquiry's costs were £14.68m, until the end of the 2024-5 financial year. Those included the salary of the chair, Sir Charles Haddon-Cave, its secretariat, lawyers and expert witnesses. The inquiry said its expenditure was proportionate and overseen judicially. However, the Ministry of Defence has given a much higher figure. Following a Freedom of Information request submitted by the BBC, the MoD put the overall cost at £58m to March 2026. The figure included the costs to the MoD as well as those of the inquiry team, it said. The MoD said that 74 of its staff were currently working more than 50% of their time on the inquiry. The SAS Regimental Association (SASRA), which represents more than 5,000 SAS veterans and serving personnel, said it remained committed to supporting the inquiry and helping achieve a "timely solution". But in a statement, it added: "The prolonged nature of the process is itself causing significant and widening harm." It said the inquiry posed a "significant challenge, not only to the regiment's reputation and the wellbeing and morale of its members, but in the association's view, to the operational effectiveness of a key element of the nation's defence". It said the cumulative effect of decades of legal scrutiny arising from operations in Northern Ireland, Iraq, Afghanistan and Syria was placing a significant burden on individuals, families and the association itself. Public inquiries are rarely quick or cheap. The Bloody Sunday Inquiry, which found the killing of 13 civil rights protesters in Northern Ireland by British soldiers was "unjustified", took 12 years to complete and cost more than £190m. In response, the inquiry said it remained committed to the welfare and safety of UK Special Forces personnel, and a timely conclusion to the inquiry was in everyone's interest. "The chair remains committed to the welfare and safety of UK Special Forces personnel and witnesses who come forward to the inquiry." title: Unmasking the gangs 'stealing millions' from UK shops
description: Policing minister Sarah Jones says the government aims to curb the impact of persistent shoplifters.
body: Leaders of the police unit say tens of thousands of pounds worth of stolen goods have been recovered The BBC has been given special access to a police unit that says it has been disrupting organised crime gangs responsible for stealing millions of pounds worth of goods from shops across the UK. The organised retail crime (ORC) team within Opal, a national police intelligence unit, was set up two years ago and works with retailers and local police forces to target criminals responsible for raids across multiple stores around Britain. It was launched after a surge in shop theft that peaked in 2025 with more than half a million offences recorded in a year. The Home Office said shoplifting offences fell last year and the charge rate rose. Opal bosses say tens of thousands of pounds worth of stolen goods have been recovered. They also say those convicted have been jailed for sentences totalling 118 years and 22 migrant criminals were deported as a result of their offences. More than 250 arrests have been made and 84 operations have been carried out since the ORCs launch in 2024. Prolific shoplifters behind more than 28,000 offences, BBC finds 'They know we're powerless': On the shoplifting front line in Greggs 'Shoplifters will take anything': Life in a theft hotspot Jim Taylor, a former detective chief superintendent who was head of Opal until August, says the organisation is targeting multiple crime gangs. "We've uncovered organised crime groups responsible for millions of pounds of theft," he said. "One of our cases impacted across 30 police forces with 57 different officers dealing with that group. Jim Taylor, former head of Opal, says one case impacted 30 police forces "We've seen foreign nationals coming to the UK, maybe considering retail theft is an easy target, low risk, high reward." He said there was anecdotal evidence of criminals travelling to the UK for a couple of days at a time to carry out what he described as "shop theft tourism". Surrey Police worked with Opal to bring down a gang in 2024 that was responsible for stealing £200,000 from Tesco stores across the country. "By having Opal in play now, we can see the collective impact across the country," said Insp Chris Thoday. "So we can get all of the offences from across the UK, deal with them as one job, and that results in tougher sentences in the courts." Stephanie Coombes, head of intelligence at Opal, said it was about enhancing cooperation between forces to target criminals operating in different parts of the country. "Where we have individual offences, often another police force won't know that another force is suffering the same offenders, so that collaborative response is much more effective," she said. Opal head of intelligence Stephanie Coombes says hundreds of arrests have been made Technology is also playing its part in the fight against organised shop theft, according to Inspector James Tribe from Thames Valley Police. "We are seeing real benefits from the likes of facial recognition among the retailers," he said. He added that it was helping police understand the geographical impact of the offending and helping forces target areas where evidence was coming from. Some police forces and businesses have also been using their own live facial recognition technology, despite concerns raised by a civil liberties group. On the shop floor, businesses have spent millions boosting their security measures. At a Co-op store in London, the BBC is shown staff wearing body cams, CCTV, a one-way system with gates and screens protecting cashiers from potential offenders. "Over the last 18 months we have seen crime come down by about 32% from its height and violence come down by about 60%," said Paul Gerrard, director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at Co-op. However, he said that despite the investment there were still too many offences. Paul Gerrard from the Co-op says offences are down but still above pre-pandemic levels "Crime is still twice what it was before the pandemic, so it is better, but against historic norms, it's still extremely high," he said. The police response to theft has been improving since 2023, he said, adding that police were now attending "seven times out of every 10". Gerrard wants the government to do more to prevent repeat offenders. "It could be employment and rehabilitation programmes, but we have to have a serious look, because the prisons will just get fuller and my colleagues in store will continue to face crime unless we tackle re-offending," he said. Last year a pilot scheme was introduced in East Sussex where a small number of persistent shoplifters were fitted with electronic tags to prevent re-offending, which is now being expanded countywide. The offender receives a criminal behaviour order and is banned from specific areas, including shops or precincts, with police monitoring for any breaches. "That gives the whole area respite because they know this offender is not allowed in," said Katy Bourne, the Sussex police and crime commissioner. Those with an addiction, would have to "go into some form of rehabilitation", Bourne added. Sussex became the first area to introduce GPS tags on prolific shoplifters Policing minister Sarah Jones says the government is looking to curb the impact of persistent shoplifters. "There is a small number of people who are responsible for a high number of shop thefts," she said. "Often they have drug addictions and other challenges that need to be addressed, but they need to know that they are going to be punished for what they've done. "Whether it's use of technology, court orders that say to them they can't come into this town centre because you are a repeat offender, we need to bear down on all of those things." title: Steve Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
description: There is no doubt over the outcome of this vote, but for the Kremlin they are still an important moment.
body: This video can not be played Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing). That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises. This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin. Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair. But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say. "We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently. That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story? For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election. This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war. I said no surprises. But there have been some. "Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV. The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns. "The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me." In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch: "The Communist Party, onwards we go! "We're with the people, don't you know?" More X Factor than exit poll. Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly: "Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!" It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war. Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine "All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament. "In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma." I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine. And if a party doesn't support the war? One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters. Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election. "The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place. "It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred." Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat. "Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel." Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism. The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down. Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election. In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine. The war is front and centre of people's minds here.
